issues.evidence: p20_wrong_shape_json: data file '[{"payer":"a"}]' -> balances crashes with KeyError: 'amount_cents' traceback (A/expense_splitter.py:44-54 checks only top-level list)
issues.summary: Load does not validate expense entries, so a well-formed but malformed JSON file crashes with a traceback.
Empty participant names are silently dropped instead of rejected.
Scientific-notation amounts are accepted, allowing surprising inputs.
Minor lint findings (raise without from, long lines).
Style lint findings, mostly old-style % formatting and long lines.

issues.evidence: B/expense_splitter.py:133-134 sorts debtor/creditor dicts every iteration
issues.summary: Settlement loop is O(n^2 log n) rather than heap-based; fine for group sizes but less efficient.

blinding_guess.why: B has a test suite, explicit data-file schema validation and a dedicated error class, consistent with a more spec-driven process.

notes: Both implementations are close: integer cents, atomic writes, greedy largest-debtor/largest-creditor settlement, and both pass all functional probes. The only probe difference is p20 (A crashes on structurally malformed entries in an otherwise valid JSON file). Probes were run with python3.11 because the system python3.9 lacks sys.stdlib_module_names for the stdlib check; programs behave identically on both. B's 9 unittest tests pass; A has no tests. CLI flags differ (A: --desc/--with, B: --description/--participants) and B uses an {"expenses": [...]} wrapper, so p20 fixtures were adapted to each side's file format.
